description: Infrastructure automation using Terraform, Ansible, CloudFormation, and IaC best practices for Java backend deployments

questions.question: What is Infrastructure as Code and what problems does it solve?
questions.answer: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) treats infrastructure configuration as code, stored in version control and applied automatically. Problems solved: 1) Manual configuration drift eliminated, 2) Reproducible environments (dev matches prod), 3) Version control for infrastructure changes, 4) Faster provisioning, 5) Documentation through code, 6) Disaster recovery simplified. Tools: Terraform, Ansible, CloudFormation, Pulumi. Example: Define AWS RDS instance in Terraform file, apply to create dev/staging/prod databases identically. Changes reviewed via PR, applied via CI/CD. Rollback possible by reverting code.

questions.question: Explain the difference between declarative and imperative IaC approaches.
questions.answer: Declarative: Define desired end state, tool figures out how to achieve it. Examples: Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes manifests. Idempotent - running multiple times produces same result. Easier to understand and maintain. Imperative: Define specific steps to reach state. Examples: Ansible (can be both), bash scripts, AWS CLI commands. More control but requires managing current state. Example declarative (Terraform): resource "aws_instance" "app" { ami = "ami-123"; instance_type = "t3.medium" } - Terraform creates or updates. Example imperative: aws ec2 run-instances followed by aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute. Most modern tools prefer declarative for predictability.

questions.question: What is Terraform and what are its core concepts?
questions.answer: Terraform is declarative IaC tool for cloud infrastructure. Core concepts: 1) Resources - infrastructure components (aws_instance, aws_rds_instance), 2) Providers - plugins for platforms (AWS, Azure, GCP), 3) State - tracks actual infrastructure, stored in backend (S3, Terraform Cloud), 4) Modules - reusable configuration blocks, 5) Variables - parameterize configurations, 6) Outputs - export values. Workflow: terraform init (download providers), terraform plan (preview changes), terraform apply (create/update infrastructure), terraform destroy (tear down). Example: Define VPC, subnets, security groups, RDS, ECS cluster for Java app. State in S3, workspaces for environments.

questions.question: How do you manage Terraform state and why is it important?
What are Terraform modules and how would you structure them for a microservices architecture?
questions.answer:
Terraform modules are reusable configuration containers. Benefits: DRY principle, standardization, simplified maintenance. Structure for microservices: Root modules for environments (prod, staging), child modules for components. Example structure:
modules/
  vpc/
  rds/
  ecs-service/
  alb/
environments/
  prod/
    main.tf
    variables.tf
  staging/
    main.tf

ecs-service module accepts variables (service_name, image, cpu, memory), creates ECS task definition, service, target group. Prod main.tf:
module "payment_service" {
  source = "../../modules/ecs-service"
  service_name = "payment"
  image = "payment:v1.2.3"
  cpu = 1024
  memory = 2048
}
module "order_service" {
  source = "../../modules/ecs-service"
  service_name = "order"
  image = "order:v1.5.0"
}
Promotes consistency, simplifies adding new services.

questions.question: Explain Ansible and how it differs from Terraform.
questions.answer:
Ansible is automation tool primarily for configuration management and application deployment. Uses YAML playbooks, agentless (SSH), imperative and declarative. Terraform focuses on infrastructure provisioning, Ansible on configuration. Key differences: 1) Terraform provisions infrastructure (create VMs, networks), Ansible configures systems (install Java, deploy apps), 2) Terraform has state, Ansible stateless, 3) Terraform declarative, Ansible playbooks often imperative. Common pattern: Terraform creates EC2 instances, Ansible playbook installs Java, Tomcat, deploys Spring Boot app. Example Ansible playbook:
- name: Deploy Spring Boot app
  hosts: app_servers
  tasks:
    - name: Install Java 17
      apt: name=openjdk-17-jdk state=present
    - name: Copy JAR
      copy: src=app.jar dest=/opt/app/
    - name: Start service
      systemd: name=app state=started
Both tools complementary in full automation stack.

questions.question: How would you implement blue-green deployment using Terraform?
questions.answer:
Blue-green deployment maintains two identical environments, switching traffic between them. Terraform implementation: Use workspaces or resource naming to differentiate. Example with AWS ECS and ALB:
1) Two ECS services (blue, green) behind same ALB with target groups,
2) ALB listener rules route traffic to active target group,
3) Deploy new version to inactive environment (green),
4) Test green environment,
5) Update Terraform to switch ALB listener to green target group,
6) Apply terraform, traffic switches instantly,
7) Keep blue for rollback.
Example:
variable "active_environment" { default = "blue" }

resource "aws_lb_listener_rule" "main" {
  action {
    type = "forward"
    target_group_arn = var.active_environment == "blue" ? 
      aws_lb_target_group.blue.arn : 
      aws_lb_target_group.green.arn
  }
}
Change active_environment to "green", apply, traffic switches. Rollback: change back to "blue".

questions.question: What is AWS CloudFormation and how does it compare to Terraform?
questions.answer:
CloudFormation is AWS-native IaC service using JSON/YAML templates. Differences from Terraform: 1) AWS-only vs multi-cloud, 2) Native AWS integration (IAM permissions, AWS support), 3) No state file (AWS manages), 4) ChangeSet preview vs terraform plan, 5) Stack management (create, update, delete as unit). CloudFormation advantages: deeper AWS integration, no separate state management, AWS Support assistance. Terraform advantages: multi-cloud, larger ecosystem, better modularity, more mature. Example CloudFormation template:
Resources:
  MyDB:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      DBInstanceClass: db.t3.medium
      Engine: postgres
      AllocatedStorage: 100
aws cloudformation create-stack deploys. Many teams use Terraform for flexibility despite CloudFormation's AWS integration benefits.

How would you provision a complete Java backend infrastructure on AWS using Terraform?
questions.answer:
Complete infrastructure includes VPC, subnets, security groups, RDS, ECS/EKS, ALB, Route53, CloudWatch. Structure:
1) VPC module: VPC, public/private subnets across AZs, NAT gateways, Internet gateway
2) RDS module: PostgreSQL Multi-AZ, subnet group, security group, parameter group
3) ECS module: Cluster, task definitions, services, auto-scaling
4) ALB module: Load balancer, target groups, listener rules, SSL certificate
5) Security groups: ALB → ECS (8080), ECS → RDS (5432)
6) Route53: DNS records pointing to ALB
7) CloudWatch: Log groups, alarms
Example main.tf:
module "vpc" {
  source = "./modules/vpc"
  cidr = "10.0.0.0/16"
}

module "rds" {
  source = "./modules/rds"
  vpc_id = module.vpc.vpc_id
  subnet_ids = module.vpc.private_subnet_ids
}

module "app" {
  source = "./modules/ecs-service"
  vpc_id = module.vpc.vpc_id
  image = "account.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/payment:v1.0.0"
  db_endpoint = module.rds.endpoint
}
terraform apply provisions complete stack. Application deployed via ECS with environment variables from Secrets Manager.

questions.question: What are Terraform providers and how do you manage provider versions?
How do you implement disaster recovery for Terraform-managed infrastructure?
questions.answer:
DR strategy for Terraform infrastructure: 1) State backups - S3 versioning enabled, lifecycle policy retains 30 days, 2) Cross-region state replication, 3) Code in git with tags for each release, 4) Separate DR region infrastructure defined in separate module/workspace, 5) Automated failover switching Route53 to DR region, 6) Regular testing (quarterly DR drills). Recovery procedure: 1) If primary region fails, verify state accessible from backup, 2) terraform workspace select dr or switch to DR directory, 3) terraform plan verify DR infrastructure correct, 4) Update Route53 to point to DR region ALB, 5) Applications continue in DR region. Prevention: RDS cross-region read replicas promoted to master, S3 replication for assets. Example: Primary us-east-1 fails, DR us-west-2 activated. Terraform configurations maintain both regions:
environments/
  prod-us-east-1/
  prod-us-west-2/
Route53 health check detects failure, failover record switches to DR. RTO: 15 minutes.

What is terraform import and how would you bring existing infrastructure under Terraform management?
questions.answer:
terraform import adds existing resources to state. Process: 1) Write resource configuration matching existing infrastructure, 2) Run terraform import to add to state, 3) Verify with terraform plan (should show no changes). Challenges: import is resource-by-resource (tedious for large infrastructures), must write configuration manually. Example: Existing RDS instance created manually:
# Write configuration
resource "aws_db_instance" "main" {
  identifier = "production-db"
  engine = "postgres"
  instance_class = "db.t3.medium"
  # ... other attributes matching existing
}

# Import
terraform import aws_db_instance.main production-db

# Verify
terraform plan # should show 0 changes

For large infrastructures, use tools: terraformer (generates Terraform code from existing infrastructure), terraform-import-generator. Alternative: rebuild infrastructure - create new stack with Terraform, migrate data, cutover. Example migration: Import 50 EC2 instances, 20 security groups, 5 load balancers. Use terraformer to auto-generate code, review/refactor, import all, verify. Gradually transition from manual to IaC management.

questions.question: How do you handle Terraform state locking failures and concurrent execution issues?
questions.answer: State locking prevents concurrent modifications. When lock fails: error message shows who holds lock and when acquired. Resolution: 1) Check if other operation running (CI/CD pipeline, teammate's apply), wait for completion, 2) If process crashed, lock remains (stale lock), verify no operation running, force unlock: terraform force-unlock <lock-id>, 3) Prevent issues: run terraform in CI/CD only, developers run plan locally, not apply. Example scenario: Developer runs terraform apply, laptop crashes, lock remains. Error: "Error acquiring the state lock". Verify no process running, terraform force-unlock abc-123-def-456. Prevention strategies: 1) DynamoDB table for locks (AWS), Azure Blob lease (Azure), 2) Short-lived locks (automatic timeout), 3) CI/CD orchestration (single source of applies), 4) Atlantis (Terraform PR automation) handles locking automatically. Example: Team uses Atlantis, developers comment 'atlantis apply' on PR, Atlantis acquires lock, applies, releases. No manual locking issues.

questions.question: Design an Ansible playbook for zero-downtime deployment of a Spring Boot application.
questions.answer:
Zero-downtime using rolling deployment. Strategy: Remove instances from load balancer, update, add back. Playbook:
---
- name: Deploy Spring Boot app with zero downtime
  hosts: app_servers
  serial: 1  # one host at a time
  tasks:
    - name: Deregister from ALB
      delegate_to: localhost
      aws_elb:
        instance_id: "{{ ec2_instance_id }}"
        state: absent
        region: us-east-1

    - name: Wait for connections to drain
      wait_for:
        timeout: 30

    - name: Stop application
      systemd:
        name: springboot-app
        state: stopped

    - name: Copy new JAR
      copy:
        src: target/app-{{version}}.jar
        dest: /opt/app/app.jar

    - name: Start application
      systemd:
        name: springboot-app
        state: started

    - name: Wait for health check
      uri:
        url: http://localhost:8080/actuator/health
        status_code: 200
      register: result
      until: result.status == 200
      retries: 10
      delay: 5

    - name: Register with ALB
      delegate_to: localhost
      aws_elb:
        instance_id: "{{ ec2_instance_id }}"
        state: present

serial: 1 ensures one server updated at a time. Remaining servers handle traffic during update.

Explain how to handle Terraform state migration when changing backend configurations.
questions.answer:
State migration moves state between backends (local → S3, S3 → Terraform Cloud). Process: 1) Backup current state, 2) Add new backend configuration, 3) terraform init -migrate-state, 4) Terraform prompts to migrate, confirm, 5) Verify new backend has state, 6) Remove old backend. Example migrating local to S3:
# Current: local state (terraform.tfstate file)

# Add backend config
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket = "company-terraform-state"
    key = "prod/terraform.tfstate"
    region = "us-east-1"
    dynamodb_table = "terraform-locks"
    encrypt = true
  }
}

# Backup
cp terraform.tfstate terraform.tfstate.backup

# Migrate
terraform init -migrate-state
# Prompt: "Do you want to copy existing state to the new backend?" → yes

# Verify
aws s3 cp s3://company-terraform-state/prod/terraform.tfstate - | head

# Test
terraform plan # should work with remote state

Changing S3 bucket: same process, Terraform copies state. Rollback: change backend config back, init -migrate-state. Critical: never delete old state until verified new backend working. Team communication essential during migration.

questions.question: How would you implement immutable infrastructure using Terraform and Packer?
Design a GitOps workflow for Terraform using Atlantis or similar tools.
questions.answer:
GitOps: infrastructure changes via git PRs, automated apply. Atlantis watches GitHub/GitLab PRs, runs Terraform. Workflow: 1) Developer creates feature branch, modifies Terraform, opens PR, 2) Atlantis automatically runs terraform plan, comments results on PR, 3) Team reviews plan and code, 4) Developer comments 'atlantis apply', 5) Atlantis runs terraform apply, comments results, 6) PR merged after successful apply. Setup:
Docker:
docker run -p 4141:4141 \
  -e ATLANTIS_REPO_ALLOWLIST='github.com/company/*' \
  -e ATLANTIS_GH_TOKEN='token' \
  -e ATLANTIS_GH_WEBHOOK_SECRET='secret' \
  runatlantis/atlantis:latest

atlantis.yaml in repo:
version: 3
projects:
- name: production
  dir: environments/prod
  autoplan:
    when_modified: ["*.tf", "*.tfvars"]
  workflow: prod-workflow

workflows:
  prod-workflow:
    plan:
      steps:
      - init
      - plan
    apply:
      steps:
      - apply

Benefits: audit trail (all changes in git), peer review before apply, automated locking, prevents concurrent applies. Example PR: add new RDS read replica, Atlantis comments plan showing new resource, team approves, 'atlantis apply' comment deploys. Alternative tools: Terraform Cloud, Spacelift, env0.

questions.question: How do you handle Terraform destroy protection for critical resources?
Explain how to manage Terraform at scale for hundreds of microservices.
questions.answer:
Scaling challenges: state management, code duplication, change coordination. Solutions: 1) Monorepo with modules - shared modules, service-specific configurations, 2) Layered architecture - foundation (VPC, networking), platform (shared services), applications (individual services), 3) State per service or logical grouping, 4) Terraform modules published to registry (GitHub, Terraform Cloud), 5) Template generation for repetitive services. Example structure:
terraform/
  modules/  # reusable
    ecs-service/
    rds/
    vpc/
  foundation/  # networking, shared
    main.tf
    terraform.tfstate
  platform/  # shared services (RDS, Redis, Kafka)
    main.tf
  services/  # individual microservices
    payment-service/
      main.tf
      terraform.tfstate
    order-service/
      main.tf
    user-service/
      main.tf

service-specific main.tf:
module "service" {
  source = "../../modules/ecs-service"
  service_name = "payment"
  image = var.image
  container_port = 8080
  health_check_path = "/actuator/health"
}

Module versioning:
module "service" {
  source = "git::https://github.com/company/terraform-modules.git//ecs-service?ref=v2.1.0"
}

CICD: changes to services/ directory trigger only affected service deployment. Terragrunt helps reduce code duplication. Team ownership: each service team manages their Terraform. Platform team owns shared modules.
